claims.text: Thermal aging of a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight HEA drives phase segregation.
Phase segregation during aging produces dispersed Mg-rich intermetallic compounds.
Mg-rich intermetallic compounds change corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior by establishing a sacrificial protective oxide layer.
The initial alloy is an as-cast, metastable single-phase solid solution with a homogeneous elemental distribution.
The initial alloy has a density below 6 g/cm3.
Aging causes Mg-rich intermetallic phases to nucleate and grow along grain boundaries and within the matrix.
Elevated temperature drives decomposition of the metastable solid solution.
The resulting Mg-rich intermetallic compounds oxidize preferentially.
Preferential oxidation of the Mg-rich intermetallic compounds forms a continuous or semi-continuous sacrificial oxide scale.
The sacrificial oxide scale enhances high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Thermally aged samples will have a refined microstructure relative to the as-cast baseline.
Thermally aged samples will contain detectable Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates relative to the as-cast baseline.
Thermally aged samples will form a more stable and adherent oxide layer during high-temperature oxidation than the as-cast baseline.
Thermally aged samples will exhibit altered corrosion rates because the evolved phases change local electrochemical behavior.
Minor alloying elements and nanoscale phase-distribution effects may influence the magnitude of corrosion and oxidation improvements.
